The increasing adoption of image-guided robot-assisted surgery (GRAS) in retinal operations has driven significant research into developing automated visual navigation systems. This paper introduces a novel method for estimating the 3D position of the eye by leveraging a single intra-operative image captured from the robot's end-effector. Our approach utilizes a single-view perspective reconstruction technique that relies on a calibrated end-effister and a pre-existing 3D eye model. By employing a 3D model to represent the eye, our method eliminates the need for time-consuming real-time tracking of the iris, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves high accuracy, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.5 mm.

We derive the $F$-polynomials associated with cluster algebras of type $A_{\infty}$ by applying the combinatorics of infinite grassmannians. This derivation yields the $F$-polynomials for the $A_{\infty}$ cluster algebras by utilizing grassmannian combinatorics.

This article explores the possibility of a future free of web passwords. Although passwordless authentication is already common, we argue that fully eliminating passwords on the internet is unlikely in the near future. We contend that the most viable path forward involves integrating passwords into a broader, flexible authentication framework.

Discrete lattice models offer a natural framework for describing systems with ultraviolet cutoffs, yet they lack a continuous momentum space, which restricts the use of established tools like Green's functions. To address this, we introduce a novel quantization method for discrete lattice models that utilizes a compact, continuous momentum space. This approach is demonstrated using the discrete Schwinger-Keldysh action for the Schwinger effect in a constant electric field. By employing a discrete path integral, we derive the continuous real-time Schwinger action and its corresponding Schwinger-Dyson equation. The continuous Green's function is then obtained by solving this equation, with the continuous spectral function extracted from the imaginary part of the Schwinger action. Our findings indicate that the continuous Green's function derived through this method aligns perfectly with the Green's function obtained directly from the discrete path integral.

The rise of autoplay in video applications has sparked significant debate regarding its impact on user agency and overall well-being. This study examines how the autoplay feature influences users' sense of control over the app, specifically within the context of a video-sharing platform. We conducted a qualitative analysis of 12 semi-interviews with participants who use the app, focusing on their perceptions of the autoplay function. Our findings indicate that while the feature is viewed as a tool that enhances user control by simplifying navigation, it can simultaneously undermine that sense of control when it restricts the user's ability to manually select content. Ultimately, these results offer critical insights for designers of video applications, highlighting the importance of integrating clear options for users to toggle the feature on or off.

This research examines the capabilities of a specific variant of Turing machines designed for reactive computation. We establish that this model is capable of simulating a universal Turing machine, thereby confirming its status as a Turing-complete computational device. We define a behaviour as "finitely executable" if it can be mirrored by a reactive Turing machine through a mapping that preserves finite traces; this concept offers a method to identify which behaviors are computable within finite limits. We demonstrate that while this model cannot generate every possible trace, it can indeed produce any finite trace. Additionally, we prove that if a behaviour is finitely executable, it can be reconstructed using a process where trace preservation remains intact. Finally, we show that if a behaviour is computable by this system, it can also be replicated by a machine that utilizes a finite set of states.

A combinatorial Gray code represents a sequential arrangement of combinatorial objects where successive elements differ by a minimal, defined alteration. This concept applies to various structures, including permutations, set partitions, and spanning trees. This work introduces a novel, efficient algorithm to generate the sequences of all valid sequences of length $n$ containing $k$ ones and $n-k$ zeros, adhering to a constraint where no more than $r$ consecutive ones appear anywhere in the sequence.

The sPHENIX experiment, a high-energy nuclear physics facility at Brookhaven National Laboratory, aims to investigate both the initial state and final state of heavy-ion collisions. Its physics program centers on measuring jet substructure and quark-gluon plasma (QGP) media response to gain insights into the QCD initial state and the QGP's transport properties. To achieve this, sPHENIX employs a comprehensive jet observables suite, including jet mass, transverse momentum, and transverse broadening, to characterize jet substructure. The detector features a central tracker, electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeters, a jet-taggered muon spectrometer, and a forward zero-degree calorimeter. This paper outlines the sPHENIX detector design and its performance in proton-proton collisions, along with the initial heavy-ion results.

This study introduces a space-time finite element framework designed for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations within deforming domains. The proposed methodology ensures conforming discretization of space-time blocks by utilizing a robust, efficient, and accurate approach to approximate the boundary integral. The work further details the formulation of a linear system, establishes the stability of the bilinear form, and demonstrates numerical findings that confirm the scheme's optimal convergence rates.

A circular flow in a signed graph is a function mapping its edges to the set of non-zero rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}^*$ such that the product of values on edges incident to any vertex equals 1. The flow index, defined as the least common multiple of these index values for all edges, is minimized for a given signed graph when considering its smallest possible circular flow. This minimum value is referred to as the circular flow index. The work herein establishes the circular flow index for several significant classes of signed graphs.

This study introduces a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm for the Modular Subset Sum problem, achieving a time complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$ with a success probability of $1 - O(n^{-1})$. The proposed method extends the deterministic polynomial-time solution by Korte and Schmidt, which is accurate for cases where the target value $s$ is non-negative.

We present a study of 1000 M dwarf stars from the LAMOST survey, utilizing a novel technique to identify flaring activity through Hα emission line profiles. This method relies on the distinct "double-peaked" shape of Hα lines observed in flaring stars, a feature that differentiates them from the single-peated profiles typical of quiescent stars. By applying this approach to the LAMOST Medium Resolution Spectra (MRS) dataset, we identified 1000 stars exhibiting flaring signatures. To validate these findings, we cross-referenced our results with the Kepler and TESS catalogs of flaring stars, achieving a 70% match rate. Furthermore, we analyzed the flare frequency distributions (FFD) of the identified sample, revealing a power-law relationship between flare energy and occurrence rate. This distribution aligns with established FFDs for both Kepler and TESS flaring stars, with a power-law index of $\alpha = 2.01 \pm 0.02$. Additionally, we examined the relationship between flare energy and stellar effective temperature, finding a positive correlation. These results confirm the efficacy of the Hα double-peaked method for detecting flaring stars and provide a comprehensive characterization of their flare frequency distributions.

Drosophila melanogaster serves as a premier model for investigating hemocyte-mediated immune responses, yet the specific mechanisms driving their development and morphogenesis remain largely unknown. This study introduces a novel, high-throughput method for analyzing hemocyte development and shape using time-lapse imaging of embryos. We demonstrate that this approach enables the precise tracking of individual hemocytes and the quantification of their morphological traits, such as area and perimeter, as well as their motility characteristics, including speed and directional persistence. Furthermore, the workflow facilitates the automated identification of apoptotic cells and the detection of cell division events. By applying this methodology to a cohort of embryos, we characterized the temporal and spatial dynamics of hemocyte development, revealing that these cells exhibit a migratory pattern consistent with chemotaxis.

This paper introduces a contrastive siamese network designed for speaker-agnostic speech recognition. The architecture comprises two identical convolutional neural networks, where the absolute difference between their outputs is fed into a fully connected layer. This layer is trained using contrastive loss to ensure that embeddings for utterances sharing the same word label are positioned closely together, while those with different labels are pushed apart. To enhance generalization, the model incorporates a regularization term that encourages embeddings from different speakers with identical labels to maintain a consistent relative distance. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech test set demonstrate a 1.5% relative reduction in word error rate (WER) compared to a baseline acoustic model, with additional improvements observed when using the proposed feature on the VoxConverse and VoxL24 datasets.

This study investigates the deep inelastic scattering (DIS) cross section for neutrinos interacting with protons, specifically within the resonance region. We introduce a novel scaling variable, $\xi_w$, which incorporates the proton's longitudinal structure function, $F_L$, and demonstrates that DIS data from the NuSea experiment at Fermilab aligns well with this variable. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the structure function $F_L$ on the $W^2$ dependence of the $\nu p \to K X$ production cross section.

This study examines the regularity of a stochastic system characterized by time-varying coefficients, where the initial state is non-stationary, and the initial state's first two moments fail to meet standard regularity requirements. A feedback mechanism is designed to enforce regularity in the adaptive control framework. Specifically, the proposed control system ensures that a unique regular process arises as a limit, with the corresponding process's mean converging to a specific solution of the associated expectation system.

The brain is often modeled as a Bayesian agent that infers its hidden state within a generative model of a dynamic world. This paper introduces a new framework called branching time active inference (BTAI), designed to capture the brain's hierarchical structure. BTAI posits that the brain's generative model is organized into a hierarchy of probabilistic state space models (PSSMs), where each level represents a distinct generative model. This architecture allows the brain to be viewed as a hierarchical agent capable of inferring its state within a multi-scale world. Furthermore, BTAI is designed to be neurally plausible, offering a potential framework for understanding how the brain implements active inference.

We investigate the transport of a localized baryon density perturbation through a quark-gluon plasma (QGP) using the holographic framework. This setup models a quench scenario where baryons are injected into a hot, deconfined medium. Our analysis examines the evolution of this baryon density lump across various initial conditions, characterized by differing masses and velocities. Our results indicate that the baryons either become trapped within the QGP or traverse it, a behavior that mirrors the experimental signatures of heavy-ion collisions.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $C(X)$ be the Tychonoff space of continuous real-valued functions on $X$. We demonstrate that if $X$ is the first-countable Tychonoff space, the locally convex space $C(X)$ is the Eberlein-Grothendieck space if and only if $X$ is the countable dense space and $X$ is the countably compact space.

This paper investigates a specific Hamiltonian system with one degree of freedom, defined by $H = \frac{1}{2}(p^2 + q^2) + \frac{1}{4}(q^2 - 1)^2$, which possesses a center at the origin. It is demonstrated that the origin functions as a center of isochronicity of order $n$ precisely when $n = 1, 2, 3, \text{or } 4$. Additionally, both numerical and analytical analyses are conducted to calculate the small oscillation frequencies and the splitting of the oscillation splitting at the origin as parameters are varied.

The Lorenz system, a cornerstone of nonlinear dynamics, is renowned for its distinctive chaotic behavior. This paper introduces a novel methodology for examining such systems, utilizing a metric termed the "similarity signature curve." This curve quantifies the degree of resemblance between the Lorenz system's dynamics and a reference sinusoidal function, $f(t) = \sin(t)$. By applying this approach, we can identify specific parameter ranges where the system exhibits periodic or quasi-periodic states, as well as instances of chaos that mirror sine-wave dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique is highly versatile, capable of analyzing systems with varying dimensions and diverse characteristics.

This study examines the linear approximation (LAN) property within a nonparametric framework for the deconvolution problem, where observations are modeled as the convolution of an unknown density with Gaussian noise. While the LAN property has been established for discrete parameter spaces in related literature, this paper extends the finding to a broader nonparametric setting. Additionally, we derive the corresponding local minimax lower bound for estimating the log-density function.

This study establishes Weyl's asymptotic law for spectra associated with non self-adjoint Laplacians acting on flat vector bundles defined over compact hyperbolic surfaces. The work also includes an analysis of Weyl's law for operators with unbounded complex potentials.

This study introduces FNetAR, a new causal language modeling algorithm that eliminates the self-attention mechanism in favor of a novel positional encoding strategy. By substituting self-attention with a Fourier transform, FNetAR achieves comparable performance to the Transformer-XL baseline (using XL-MaxLength = 512) while reducing computational costs by 50%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed Fourier-based positional encoding surpasses the standard Hamming encoding in terms of effectiveness.

This study examines the transition from the universe's deceleration to its current acceleration phase, utilizing a model where the universe is filled with a scalar field possessing a time-dependent coupling to matter. The findings indicate that a transition epoch can occur within a finite time duration, contingent upon the specific form of the time-dependent coupling.

We examine the phase diagram of a two-dimensional superconductor with disorder, which exhibits distinct phases including a diffusive thermal metal, a topological superconductor, and a thermal insulator. Our analysis reveals a phase transition occurring between the topological superconducting state and the thermal insulator state, characterized by a transition between a Fermi-arc edge state and a topological thermal insulator edge state. This transition is driven by a shift in the topological invariant, specifically the topological central charge.

The concept of a "depression epidemic" has gained significant attention, with numerous studies linking social media usage to depressive symptoms. This research examines the relationship between online discussions of happiness and depression, revealing a strong correlation between the pursuit of happiness and the experience of depression.

Dark matter remains a significant unsolved issue in astrophysics, with various candidates proposed to explain its nature. Among these, the lightest R-parity violating superpartner is a particularly intriguing theoretical possibility. This study examines the detection prospects for such dark matter using the XENON1T experiment, which utilizes a 1.2-ton liquid xenon time projection chamber. We calculate the nuclear recoil energy distributions for dark matter-nucleus interactions and evaluate their compatibility with the observed data. Our analysis indicates that the experiment excludes dark matter masses below 10 GeV for singlet models and below 5 GeV for doublet models, assuming a coupling constant of $\lambda_{\rm DM-X} \geq 10^{-3}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the XENON1T data effectively rules out the parameter space of the $\lambda_{\rm DM-X} \geq 10^{-3}$ region for dark matter masses under 10 GeV.

The magnetic properties of the spin-1 chain compound Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_6$ were investigated using neutron diffraction and polarized neutron powder diffraction. Below the Néel temperature of 10.5 K, the Ni$^{2+}$ moments arrange into a commensurate, long-range antiferromagnetic order characterized by a (1,0,0) propagation vector. This structure comprises two distinct Ni sublattices with distinct magnetic moments: one aligned along the a-axis and the other along the b-axis. Furthermore, the magnetic Bragg peaks associated with the a-sublattice are significantly more intense than those from the b-sublattice. The experimental findings are consistent with a model describing the Ni sublattices as two distinct, weakly interacting spin-1 chains.

The rapid proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced a complex array of data sources, creating significant challenges for network trust. A primary obstacle is the inherent uncertainty across diverse and often conflicting data streams, which hampers the ability to establish reliable trust. To address this, we introduce a framework designed to evaluate trustworthiness by integrating uncertainty metrics. This approach employs a Bayesian network to model uncertainty, which feeds into a hierarchical trust architecture. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through a case study involving a smart home environment.

Spline interpolation is widely employed in computational physics, yet it can exhibit the Gibbs phenomenon, leading to spurious oscillations near discontinuities. This study introduces a novel method for computing piecewise polynomial interpolations that effectively suppresses these oscillations. The approach involves adding a penalty term to the standard least-squares minimization for splines, ensuring the resulting solution remains a minimizer of a modified objective function. This modification constrains the magnitudes of spline coefficients to adhere to a user-defined bound, thereby guaranteeing that interpolated functions stay within a specific band around the target function. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of this technique, along with numerical experiments demonstrating its performance.

This study examines four-dimensional Taub-NUT solutions within $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{E} + \lambda \phi^4$ theory, specifically focusing on the geometry of the Einstein tensor components. We analyze the spacetime's curvature singularities and asymptotic limits, revealing that these solutions encompass both black holes and cosmological models. Furthermore, we investigate the space of parameters governing these Taub-NUT geometries to identify a specific configuration where a black hole solution emerges.

In Information Retrieval (IR) contexts, accurately labeling multimedia content is crucial for training and assessing models. This paper introduces a comprehensive dataset of 1.2 million images, each annotated with a precise count of people present. We detail the dataset's creation methodology and performance benchmarks, including results from our proposed counting model. Additionally, we examine the inherent difficulties associated with counting individuals within images and highlight the dataset's potential value for advancing research in computer vision.

The interplay between competition and random drift is a primary driver of biodiversity within large ecosystems. While numerous theoretical frameworks have addressed this interaction, they typically focus on small populations, where stochastic effects are significant, or on scenarios where only one mechanism is dominant. In this study, we examine a model of a large, finite ecosystem where both forces are significant, utilizing a system of replicating species with varying sizes. Our approach employs a multi-scale analysis to derive a limiting partial differential equation describing the evolution of species size distributions. Our findings indicate that the system's long-term behavior is governed by a balance between competition and drift, leading to a stable distribution that preserves diversity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's long-term dynamics are independent of initial conditions, provided the initial distribution is sufficiently close to the equilibrium.

Network attacks are prevalent in both natural and artificial networks, with a primary focus on node-based strategies involving addition, deletion, or modification. A defining characteristic of these attacks is the "avalanche" effect, where a minor alteration triggers disproportionately large consequences. Although extensive research has examined various attack types, the specific influence of the timing of these changes remains largely unexplored. This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing temporal network attacks, utilizing a time-dependent graph model to evaluate how the timing of node removals impacts the resulting avalanche magnitude. The analysis covers diverse real-world networks, including power grids, power grids, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The results demonstrate that the size of the avalanche is highly sensitive to the timing of node removals, with the duration of this influence varying across different network types.

This paper introduces a method for generating questions that probe deep textual understanding. Unlike surface-level queries, these require readers to synthesize information across the entire document to find answers. Our approach involves extracting answer spans from the text and formulating inquiries around them. To achieve this, we employ a two-stage pipeline: first, we use a BERT-based model to identify semantically diverse spans, followed by an encoder-decoder architecture to generate questions targeting those specific segments. Second, we introduce a self-BLEU refinement strategy to diversify question phrasings for each span. Evaluated on the SemEval 2016 Question Generation (QNLI) dataset, our model attains an F1 score of 40.19.

This study addresses the numerical solution of time-harmonic wave propagation problems by employing Perfectly Matched Layers (PML) to truncate the computational domain. We introduce a novel family of nonconforming finite element methods tailored for PML-discretized domains, which are further discretized using the Crouzeix-Raviart finite element space. The analysis demonstrates that the error in the H¹-norm is bounded by O(h^{3/2}) relative to the mesh size h, provided the mesh is quasi-uniform. Additionally, we establish that the error in the L²-norm is bounded by O(h^{5/2}) under the same quasi-uniform condition.

This study investigates the fluid dynamics of an array of droplets subjected to a sudden pressure impulse. The researchers examined how the interplay between surface tension and viscous forces governs the collective behavior of the system, specifically by manipulating the spatial periodicity of the array and the initial velocity of the liquid-liquid interface. The results indicate that the droplets' response is characterized by a sequence of distinct stages, which are analyzed through a combination of experimental observations and numerical simulations.

The Internet of Things (IoT) has become a vital component of modern life, with billions of devices now interconnected. As IoT expands, it is increasingly integrated into critical sectors like healthcare, finance, and transportation, where Quality of Service (QoS) is paramount. Consequently, the surge in IoT traffic demands that the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks collaborate to ensure QoS for these applications. This study introduces a novel QoS assurance framework for 5G-IoT that leverages the capabilities of Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV). The proposed framework utilizes a centralized SDN controller to manage traffic and enforce QoS policies, while NFV supplies the necessary network functions to support IoT services. To ensure QoS, the system employs a dynamic resource allocation strategy that adjusts NFV instance placement based on IoT traffic patterns. Additionally, the framework incorporates a self-healing mechanism to detect and resolve NFV failures, ensuring continuous service availability.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the protoplanetary disk surrounding the young star TW Hydrae, which exhibits a prominent gap and a trailing spiral arm. Utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we obtained high-resolution images of the disk's continuum emission at 3.1 and 3.4 millimeters, as well as the $^{13}$CO and C$^{17}$O rotational lines at 3.6 millimeters. Our data reveal that the disk's dust continuum emission displays a gap and a spiral structure that align closely with those seen in the millimeter-sized dust and gas emissions. We fitted the continuum data with a simple model featuring a single gap and a single spiral arm, determining that the gap's location and width are consistent with those observed in the gas. By applying the Rossiter-Light effect to the spectral line profiles, we constrained the mass of the perturbing body to be between 10 and 15 Jupiter masses ($M_{\rm Jup}$). Furthermore, we measured the gas-to-dust mass ratio in the disk to be approximately 100, a value that is roughly 10 times lower than the cosmic average. These findings suggest that the observed gap and spiral arm in the TW Hydrae disk are caused by a massive planet, which is likely responsible for the observed depletion of dust.

This study introduces a vector-valued distance metric for $ n \times n $ symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, offering a more comprehensive analysis than scalar-valued alternatives. We demonstrate that this vector-valued approach can be derived from a positive definite bilinear form on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Additionally, we establish a framework to define a partial ordering among vectors of such distances.

The increasing volatility of renewable energy sources has highlighted the need for flexible energy storage solutions. This study investigates the potential of a hydrogen network to balance supply fluctuations by converting renewable electricity into hydrogen via electrolysis, distributing it through a gas grid, and subsequently converting it back to electricity using a fuel cell. A stochastic optimization framework is developed to determine the optimal deployment of these conversion units, accounting for uncertainties in renewable generation and energy demand. The research evaluates the network's performance across various configurations of assets, asset locations, and grid topologies. Results indicate that a hydrogen network can effectively mitigate supply variability, yielding up to a 10% increase in renewable energy utilization. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that a single stochastic optimization model can effectively address diverse network scenarios.

We introduce a novel technique for estimating the orientation of horizontal magnetic fields beneath the surface by analyzing travel time anisotropy in shear wave splitting. This approach is particularly effective for regions where subsurface anisotropy is primarily driven by subsurface horizontal magnetic fields, though it remains sensitive to other anisotropic sources. By applying this method to the central United States, we derived the orientation of the horizontal magnetic field from the travel time anisotropy observed in shear wave splitting. Our findings demonstrate a strong correlation between the magnetic field's orientation and the azimuth of fast shear waves, with the magnetic field direction accounting for 60% to 70% of the observed anisotropy. This relationship holds true for both the direction and the magnitude of the variations in anisotropy across different locations. Consequently, this method offers a practical means to quantify the degree of anisotropy caused by subsurface horizontal magnetic fields.

This paper addresses the challenge of guiding a drone from an initial to a target waypoint within the shortest possible time. We model the drone's propulsion as a constant-magnitude force, allowing for free orientation, and assume the vehicle adheres to Newton's second law. By applying Pontryagin's minimum principle, we derive the optimal control law and demonstrate that the optimal strategy involves alternating between maximum thrust and zero thrust. Furthermore, we calculate the optimal travel time and provide numerical simulations to validate the proposed approach.

This study examines the equivalence of additive conjugacy codes over the field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ with linear cyclic codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$. We establish a direct correspondence between a specific family of codes over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ and cyclic codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$ by defining the corresponding $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-based additive conjugacy codes. Additionally, we derive the generator matrices for these codes.

Physicists seeking employment face significant challenges, particularly at community colleges and institutions heavily focused on undergraduate education, where their professional expertise is often underutilized. This work outlines strategies for physicists to secure positions at such departments while ensuring their disciplinary knowledge is effectively integrated into the curriculum.

These findings align with the predictions of the Standard Model.

We present the leading-order calculations for the twist-2 and twist-3 D-meson distribution amplitudes alongside their corresponding evolution kernels. Leveraging these results, we compute the twist-2 and twist-3 branching fractions for the $B \to D\pi l\nu$ decay process.

This paper investigates the spectra of power hypergraphs by establishing connections between their eigenvalues and those of signed subgraphs within their base graphs. We derive explicit formulas for the eigenvalues of $K_{n_1,\dots,n_m}^{r}$—the $r$-th power of the complete $m$-partite graph—and for the $r$-th power of a complete hypergraph. Additionally, we characterize the spectrum of the complete tripartite hypergraph $K_{n_1,n_2,n_3}^2$ when $n_1 \le n_2 \le n_3$. The study further examines the spectra of signed hypergraphs derived from signed complete bipartite graphs and the $K_4$-signed graph, deriving formulas for their eigenvalues.

The global expansion of satellite-based services is driving the deployment of massive satellite constellations. To enhance the capabilities of individual platforms, the concept of cooperative localization is gaining traction. This approach enables satellites to exchange position data with one another to refine their own orbital determination. This study examines the potential of utilizing such cooperation for large-scale constellations. We introduce a novel method for cooperative localization that integrates data from inter-satellite links (ISLs) and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) within a single, unified framework. By leveraging this joint processing, the proposed strategy aims to minimize the computational burden on each satellite and reduce the total amount of telemetry traffic required.

We report the discovery of a transiting hot Jupiter, WASP-121b, which exhibits transit timing variations (TTVs) indicative of orbital migration. This system consists of a G-type star with a mass of 1.03 ± 0.02 solar masses and a radius of 1.11 ± 0.02 solar radii, orbiting a Jupiter-mass planet at a period of 1.41 days. Our analysis of 14 years of data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and 10 years of ground-based observations reveals a transit timing residual of 1.4 ± 0.2 days, with a period of 1.4 ± 0.1 years. This variability suggests the planet migrated inward from beyond the star's corotation radius, likely driven by tidal interactions with the convective zone of the host star. This system represents the first confirmed case of a hot Jupiter exhibiting TTVs with a period of less than 2 years, providing a unique opportunity to study the orbital evolution of hot Jupiters.

This study introduces a novel calibration approach for the 21-cm power spectrum, utilizing a neural network to refine the foreground removal process. By employing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to separate foregrounds from the 21-cm signal, we demonstrate that the method's sensitivity and precision are enhanced through the incorporation of additional information regarding the training data. Specifically, the network is supplied with the raw channel power spectrum alongside a mask identifying foreground-dominated regions. This masking technique, which leverages the known spatial distribution of foregrounds, allows the network to distinguish between foreground and 21-cm signals more effectively. Our results indicate that this strategy significantly boosts the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for the 21-cm power spectrum. Furthermore, we validate the technique's robustness by training the network on simulations with varying foreground distributions and successfully applying it to data from the EDGES experiment.

Let $G$ be a connected compact Lie group, and let $X$ denote an algebraic $G$-Kahler manifold (an algebraic $G$-manifold equipped with holomorphic symplectic structure) that admits a moment map $\mu: X \to \mathfrak{g}^*$. Suppose $E$ and $E'$ are $G$-equivariant vector bundles over $X$ such that their equivariant Chern classes coincide, i.e., $c^G_E = c^G_{E'}$. We demonstrate that $E$ and $E'$ are isomorphic as $G$-equivariant bundles. This result is established by examining the fibers of the moment map $\mu$. Specifically, we establish that the isomorphism class of the equivariant bundle $E$ is fully determined by the isomorphism classes of its fibers $E_x$ for all $x \in \mu^{-1}(\operatorname{reg}(\mu))$, where $\operatorname{reg}(\mu)$ denotes the regular values of $\mu$. Furthermore, we show that the bundle $E$ is isomorphic to $E'$ if and only if the associated $G$-equivariant bundles over the fibers of $\mu$ are isomorphic.

The prime number theorem (PNT) is a foundational theorem in analytic number theory that describes the asymptotic behavior of the prime-counting function. In 1914, S. Chowla provided a simplified, self-contained proof of the PNT based on elementary principles. This work extends Chowla's approach by deriving a "stronger" version of the PNT, which establishes a logarithmic error term within the prime-counting function estimate.

Mixed models featuring categorical time are commonly employed in clinical trials to analyze repeated measures data. However, treating time categories as fixed factors necessitates estimating separate parameters for each visit, which can inflate the model's degrees of freedom consumption and lead to low statistical power. Additionally, this approach often yields inaccurate p-values and confidence intervals when the number of time points is large. To address these limitations, we propose a novel method for modeling repeated measures data by integrating the advantages of both continuous and categorical time approaches. This technique utilizes a continuous time framework to estimate a standard linear mixed model with a single slope, while simultaneously incorporating a categorical time effect to capture specific visit-level deviations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulation studies and apply it to a clinical trial dataset.

This study introduces a crowdsourcing-based routing algorithm designed for connected vehicles. The approach leverages real-time vehicle telemetry to identify traffic bottlenecks and utilizes crowd participation incentives to encourage drivers to share their routes. The algorithm's performance is benchmarked against a baseline method that relies exclusively on historical traffic data. Simulation results indicate that our proposed method outperforms the baseline by reducing total travel time by up to 10% and increasing network capacity by up to 5%.

Recent research indicates that models achieving better generalization often possess flat minima, yet this metric fails to account for scenarios where test data differs from training data. This study investigates the link between the landscape of neural network minima and generalization when the training and test datasets originate from distinct distributions. We demonstrate that even when models with flatter minima exhibit superior generalization on the training set, they may perform worse on the training set. This work examines the relationship between neural network minimizers and generalization across different training and testing data distributions. This work introduces a new approach to mitigate electromagnetic interference (EMI) in wireless radios by utilizing compact, reflective diode-based parametric frequency selective limiters (RFSLs). Unlike traditional absorbing RF filters, these reflective devices offer a more efficient power profile. The proposed RFSL architecture employs a two-stage design that integrates a frequency-selective series inductor with frequency-selective series capacitors. The authors present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the RFSL's transmission and reflection characteristics, supported by experimental data from a two-stage prototype. The study also outlines design guidelines for optimizing the RFSL's performance and validates the proposed model through a three-stage prototype implementation.

This study introduces a stochastic model for infectious diseases that accounts for heterogeneous population susceptibility and variable transmission rates. We establish the existence of an epidemic threshold based on a basic reproduction ratio and determine conditions under which the disease either vanishes or persists. Furthermore, we analyze how the probability of persistence evolves as it relates to the threshold parameter.

We present a straightforward, scalable, and effective unsupervised method for creating vector representations of phrases, building upon existing techniques for word vectors. This approach leverages the distributional hypothesis, which posits that a phrase's semantic meaning is reflected in the contexts shared with semantically similar phrases. Additionally, we demonstrate that phrase vector representations can be generated by aggregating (averaging) vector representations of constituent words. These proposed representations perform comparably to those derived from neural networks on various downstream tasks, including phrase similarity estimation and phrase classification.

This paper examines the number of components of order $k$ within a random geometric graph $G(n,r)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $n$ represents the vertex count, $r$ denotes the link radius, and connections exist between vertices separated by a distance no greater than $r$. For a fixed $k$, the variance of the component count grows linearly with $n$ at the same scale as the mean, provided $r$ is set to $r_n = s n^{-1/d}$ for any $s>0$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the variance's growth rate is determined by the expected number of components of order $k$ having a vertex at the origin in a Poisson process with intensity $s$ over the unit ball $B_d$.

We introduce a new method for numerically solving the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars, which employs a Lagrangian framework where the computational grid deforms alongside the star. This approach is combined with a finite volume technique for angular momentum, ensuring its strict conservation. Our study applies this technique to study equilibrium configurations of differentially rotating stars, which are governed by the Hall viscosity. This work is the first to investigate the Hall viscosity's impact on stellar equilibrium structures. Our results demonstrate that the inclusion of Hall viscosity significantly impacts the shape of rotating stars, particularly in the presence of differential rotation.

This study examines a generalized Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime, defined as spherically symmetric solutions to Einstein's field equations where the source consists of a perfect fluid with variable density and pressure. We analyze a specific case where the energy density and pressure depend solely on the radial coordinate, $r$. By employing a hydrodynamic framework, we derive the corresponding equations of state and investigate the resulting conditions for the causality and stability of the fluid. Furthermore, we compare this generalized model with standard LTB spacetime regarding its thermodynamic behavior, particularly focusing on the evolution of the fluid as it approaches the singularity.

Web user behavior is vital for online businesses, as it offers valuable insights into customer needs and site effectiveness. This research introduces a new concept called "visit intention," which refers to a user's specific goal for their current visit. We present a method to automatically identify this intention by leveraging the user's navigation path and the textual content of the web page. Our approach utilizes a user path to forecast the most probable intention, while also employing a user profile to generate a prior probability distribution across potential intentions. We evaluated our method on a real-world dataset comprising 1,000 users and 1,000 sessions from a travel agency website. The results indicate that our technique surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, with performance gains becoming more pronounced as the user profile becomes more specific.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology for enhancing wireless communication. However, existing RIS designs typically rely on reflective elements, which restrict their application in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios. To address this, this paper introduces the concept of transmissive RIS (TRIS) and investigates its performance within a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) framework. We analyze the achievable rate for both TRIS and conventional RIS (RIS) systems, demonstrating that TRIS can significantly outperform RIS in specific conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a low-complexity algorithm for beamforming design that leverages the specific architecture of TRIS. Simulation results confirm that this proposed TRIS architecture combined with the designed beamforming algorithm can substantially improve system performance.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to optimize policies using only static datasets, avoiding any new interactions with the environment. This approach is particularly valuable in safety-critical domains like healthcare, where data scarcity and the high cost of mistakes drive the need for training on existing records. However, offline RL faces a critical challenge: distributional shift, which arises when the offline data distribution diverges from the distribution encountered by an agent's policy. This mismatch can lead to catastrophic overfitting, where models perform well on observed data but fail or act dangerously on unseen states. To address this, we introduce a novel method called "Offline RL with Offline Distribution Matching" (O-RMD). The core idea is to explicitly model and minimize the distribution shift between offline data and the learned policy during training. By incorporating distribution matching as a regularization term, O-RMD effectively penalizes the policy for drifting toward unobserved states. Empirical results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that O-RMD consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior performance with greater stability.

We present an innovative method for automatically deriving free theorems of a specific polymorphic function from its type alone. Our approach is demonstrated through cases of polymorphic functions with simple types, showcasing the method's effectiveness in various scenarios.

We report the discovery of a new galaxy, J0437+2456, located at a redshift of $z=0.024$, which exhibits a redshift consistent with the local universe. This galaxy is situated approximately 100 arcseconds from the quasar SDSS J1025+2450, a quasar with a redshift of $z=0.031$. The galaxy's recession velocity is measured at $v_{\rm rec}=1000$ km/s, indicating that it is receding from the quasar.

This study examines the singularities of the generalised three-body problem, specifically focusing on configurations where three equal-mass bodies are arranged in a straight line. We demonstrate that these linear arrangements function as generalised syzygies; notably, if one such syzygy occurs, every subsequent trajectory passing through that point becomes confined to a specific invariant surface. We establish the existence of numerous such configurations and categorise them based on the corresponding invariant surfaces. Furthermore, we propose a numerical method to compute solutions that remain on these surfaces.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) offers a distinct advantage over standard fluorescence imaging by providing information regarding the local microenvironment of fluorophores. This capability is particularly valuable for biological applications, where it aids in distinguishing between healthy and diseased tissues. However, the utility of FLIM is often constrained by the time-intensive nature of data acquisition and the computational burden associated with processing. This study introduces a new deep learning framework designed to reconstruct FLIM images from raw photon counts. The proposed method employs a U-Net architecture, where the input consists of a series of images representing photon counts at varying exposure durations, and the output is a corresponding fluorescence lifetime image. The system was trained on a dataset of 1000 simulated FLIM images, and its performance was validated against experimental data from three distinct biological samples. The results demonstrate that the reconstructed FLIM images exhibit high fidelity, with the model achieving a mean squared error of 0.0014 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 11.47.

Personalized product search is a critical component of modern e-commerce, yet existing methods often fail to adequately account for the diverse nature of user preferences. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to model these varied preferences by integrating both explicit and implicit signals. Specifically, we combine item-level signals derived from product attributes with session-level signals based on user behavior. To achieve this, we develop a new deep learning architecture called Deep Hybrid Preference Network (DHPN). This network utilizes a hybrid attention mechanism to capture both local and global interactions, thereby learning comprehensive user preferences. Empirical evaluations on a real-world e-commerce dataset demonstrate that DHPN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

Graph embedding is a critical area of research, yet the stability of learned representations remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework for graph embedding that leverages a dual-stream architecture to enhance stability. The first stream utilizes a contrastive learning approach to ensure the stability of node embeddings, while the second employs a generative model to capture the underlying graph structure. We further propose a new loss function that integrates both streams to balance the stability of node embeddings with the accuracy of graph structure recovery. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Grant-free access is a pivotal technology for enabling massive machine-type communications, allowing devices to transmit data without prior scheduling or random access procedures. This study investigates grant-free uplink communications in multi-cell environments featuring inter-cell interference. We introduce a joint estimation framework for channel and data detection that leverages a sparse Bayesian learning approach. This method employs a shared global prior for channels across all cells and individual local priors to refine channel estimates based on local observations. Furthermore, we develop a message passing algorithm to jointly recover signals and channels, utilizing the shared global and local sparsity structures. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed scheme achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a novel method for compressed sensing that utilizes a sparse coding matrix. By integrating a sparse coding matrix into the sampling matrix, we can derive the original signal from fewer measurements than necessary. The proposed approach is validated through experiments on both synthetic data and MRI images. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sparse coding strategy significantly enhances the performance of iterative algorithms used for image reconstruction.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in handling complex tasks, particularly when sufficient labeled data is available. However, their performance often degrades significantly in data-scarce scenarios, such as those encountered in medical imaging. To address this limitation, recent research has focused on data augmentation techniques to expand available training data. While traditional augmentation methods rely on deterministic transformations, this paper proposes a novel approach leveraging randomness to generate diverse samples. By utilizing a random variable to define the augmentation process, we can employ the resulting random samples as input for training a generative model. Subsequently, samples generated by this trained model serve as data augmentation during the training of a classification network. We demonstrate that this strategy, which integrates a generative model with a classifier, effectively improves the performance of DNNs in domain adaptation and out-of-distribution generalization.

This paper investigates the Jordan ring of self-adjoint matrices within a complex Hilbert space, demonstrating that every 2-local inner derivation of this Jordan ring corresponds to a derivation. Furthermore, we establish that if a Hilbert space has a dimension greater than 2, the Jordan ring of self-adjoint operators is completely characterized by its 2-locally inner derivations.

Berry's phase represents a geometric phase resulting from a system's adiabatic evolution within a parameter space, a concept that has been extensively studied in quantum mechanics. In this work, we investigate the Berry's phase arising from adiabatically varying the parameters of a single-mode squeezed state. We demonstrate that this phase manifests in both the wave function and the density matrix, and we further examine the influence of a parametric amplifier's initial state on the Berry's phase.

This study examines the existence and stability of matter waves within binary Bose-Einstein mixtures that are subject to a periodic potential and exhibit inter- and intra-species interactions. We establish that under these conditions, the system supports compactons, defined as solutions featuring finite widths alongside infinite tails. Our analysis demonstrates that the existence and stability of these compactons are contingent upon the periodic potential's amplitude and the magnitude of inter-species interactions. Furthermore, the compacton tails are shown to be tunable via adjustments to the detuning frequency and intra-species interaction strengths. We also investigate the stability of these compactons using linear stability analysis, revealing that they remain stable when subjected to both inter- and intra-species interactions.

This study demonstrates that within the space of functions defined on $[0,1] \times \mathbb{R}$, any continuous function can be approximated by a smooth function belonging to a specific parabolic class of weighted spaces, provided it meets certain conditions. Furthermore, the proof establishes that a similar result holds true for the unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$.

We examine the phenomenology of axion-like particles (ALPs) interacting with Standard Model gauge bosons through non-renormalizable dimension-five operators. This framework encompasses both the well-known model featuring a dimension-six operator alongside a renormalizable dimension-five operator, as well as more general scenarios where the dimension-six term is absent. Our analysis covers both perturbative and non-perturbative regimes. By utilizing the existing framework of the Effective Field Theory of Axions (EFToA), we map out the relevant phenomenological signatures and establish constraints on the ALP parameter space from recent searches conducted at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This study introduces a hardware and software collaborative approach designed to enhance the performance of general-purpose processors. The methodology involves developing a specialized instruction set that enables efficient, parallel execution of specific matrix operations, which are then integrated into the instruction-level architecture. The core of this framework is a novel matrix multiplication instruction that leverages a programmable hardware accelerator to perform the computation. The accelerator is built upon a 3D mesh topology, where each processing element (PE) is a configurable unit capable of executing either a multiply or an add operation. The proposed instruction set architecture (ISA) is expanded to accommodate instructions for data movement and memory access, ensuring seamless interaction between the hardware units and processor registers. The study details the design and implementation of the accelerator, including its synthesis results, and evaluates the overall performance of the system.

Deep neural networks trained on extensive image collections have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across numerous computer vision domains, including object detection, segmentation, and classification. However, these models are typically resource-intensive, necessitating substantial computational power and memory. To address this, we introduce a method for constructing a compact neural network that closely replicates the output of a larger target model. This approach employs a two-stage process: first, a deep embedding network is trained to map the large model's outputs into a lower-dimensional space; subsequently, a new network is trained to approximate the output of this embedding model. This strategy facilitates the creation of smaller architectures that achieve high fidelity to the original large model's behavior. We evaluate this technique on various tasks, such as image classification and semantic segmentation, and further investigate its application in domain adaptation.

This paper examines a singular quasi-linear elliptic system featuring a non-homogeneous $p(x)$-Laplacian, defined over a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We establish the existence of solutions using truncation methods alongside the Schauder fixed point theorem. Subsequently, we analyze the existence and multiplicity of positive solutions by applying the Krein-Rutman theorem, which relies on the properties of the resolvent operator associated with the system's homogeneous counterpart.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are widely utilized for tasks involving long-term dependencies, yet training them remains challenging due to issues like the vanishing and exploding gradient problems. While recent research has focused on improving the approximation of long-term dependencies, the critical issue of gradient instability has received less attention. This paper introduces a novel architecture called the Gated Graph Identity (GGi) network, which is designed to mitigate both vanishing and exploding gradients. The GGi mechanism ensures that the gradient of the output with respect to the previous state remains either identical to or a scaled version of the previous state's gradient, effectively constraining gradient magnitude. Additionally, the proposed architecture incorporates a residual connection that facilitates the direct transmission of information from the previous state to the current one. Empirical results on the Penn Treebank and character-level synthetic data demonstrate that the GGi network outperforms existing methods, achieving faster training speeds and better accuracy.

This study addresses the ergodic case of Markov Decision Processes (MDP) with unbounded rewards, where the objective is to maximize the long-term average reward. While existing literature on ergodic MDPs typically assumes a countable state space, we specifically examine scenarios with an uncountable state space. Additionally, we relax the common assumption of irreducibility by allowing the system to be reducible, provided that every state can reach a target state within finite steps. Our analysis covers both the existence of stationary optimal policies and the convergence of a generalized policy iteration algorithm.

This study demonstrates the generation of a circularly polarized electron pulse with a duration of 100 picoseconds using a spin-selective optical cavity. This study proposes a novel mathematical model of living systems based on the hypothesis that a fundamental, universal mechanism drives the evolution of complexity. This hypothesis is encapsulated in a vital scalar field equation, which governs the temporal progression of complexity. The authors demonstrate that this framework is capable of modeling the growth of complexity in organisms, ranging from unicellular life to humans. Furthermore, the authors illustrate how the proposed model can be utilized to construct a theoretical representation of the human body.

The global shift toward an evidence-based approach to Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) policy necessitates open access to research outputs. This transition is driven by the need for a more robust, transparent, and accountable system, which in turn requires a deeper understanding of the socio-technical frameworks that shape policy. This paper examines the socio-technical architecture of STI policy in South and East Asia, with a specific focus on South Korea, Japan, and China. We analyze the current landscape of open access to research outputs within these nations, highlighting the pivotal role of national funding agencies in establishing open access mandates. Furthermore, we explore the specific mechanisms and strategies employed by these agencies to advance open access goals. The study concludes by addressing the broader implications of these findings for science, technology, and innovation policy in the region.

This study examines the camera's security implications by analyzing the visual content it processes. The Ethereum blockchain, serving as a decentralized platform for applications and smart contracts, has seen a surge in user adoption, prompting the need to analyze how account types interact within the network. This study examines the transactional behavior of externally owned accounts (EOCs) and contract accounts (CAs) by analyzing their network structures and identifying distinct groups based on transactional similarities. By applying network science and machine learning techniques, we map the topological features of EOCs and CAs, utilizing these attributes to classify accounts into clusters. Our findings reveal that account types within specific clusters exhibit consistent transaction patterns, while the network positions of EOCs and CAs differ significantly across clusters. Furthermore, we successfully identified CAs with particular functionalities, such as those used for initial coin offerings (ICOs) and those facilitating private transactions.

We report on the investigation of light-induced changes in the two-dimensional electron system at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface, a phenomenon that alters both carrier density and mobility. Our findings indicate that the sheet resistance decreases under illumination, a behavior consistent with an increase in carrier density. Furthermore, we observe that the sheet resistance exhibits a negative temperature coefficient at low temperatures, a trend that becomes more pronounced as light intensity rises.

This work investigates the computational complexity of BV logic, the framework for logics that are not first-order. We demonstrate that provability within BV logic corresponds to a $\mathsf{D}$-complete problem, a classification situated between NP and PSPACE. Furthermore, we establish that the satisfiability problem in BV logic is $\mathsf{D}$-hard, a result that encompasses the previously known $\mathsf{D}$-hardness for propositional logic.

This study examines the fundamental identity governing quantum dilogarithms, known as the pentagon identity. We establish an asymptotic expansion for the limit of quantum dilogarithms as their deformation parameter approaches zero, wherein the q-deformed case reduces to its classical q → 1 analog.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to estimate photometric redshifts (photo-zs) for galaxies, utilizing a hybrid of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). This approach leverages the CNN's capacity to extract spatial features from galaxy images and employs an MLP to map these features to photometric redshifts. Our model was trained and evaluated using the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Subaru Strategic Program dataset, which includes photometric redshifts derived from the Subaru Strategic Program (SSP) and the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC). The results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing techniques, particularly in reducing systematic biases and random errors across a wide range of redshifts. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that incorporating multi-band photometric data significantly enhances the accuracy of photo-z estimates.

Gaussian Process emulators are widely utilized to approximate complex computer models, particularly in scenarios where the models are computationally expensive or their analytical solutions are inaccessible. This paper introduces a new approach to Gaussian Process emulation that integrates the principles of the method of double emulators. Specifically, we develop a double emulator framework where the computer model and a Gaussian Process model of the computer model are emulated simultaneously. This double emulator formulation is subsequently simplified to derive a novel, streamlined Gaussian Process model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through two case studies: one involving a simple benchmark problem and another addressing a more complex scenario with a partial differential equation.

We introduce a quantum classical density-matrix renormalization group (QC-DMRG) approach designed to tackle the one-dimensional Hubbard model. By utilizing a quantum computer to compute the reduced two-particle density matrix, we perform renormalization based on the Coulomb interaction, employing a bond dimension of $D=2$. This method successfully achieves convergence to the exact ground state within the thermodynamic limit for two-electron systems. In systems with three electrons, QC-DMRG yields results that align closely with exact solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's viability on a trapped ion quantum processor, successfully identifying the ground state of the Hubbard model on a four-site linear chain.

We introduce a novel extension of the Standard Model featuring a non-Abelian gauge symmetry $SU(2)_X$ and a corresponding triplet of new gauge bosons, denoted as $X^0$, $X^+$, and $X^{++}$. This framework also incorporates a new scalar field, $X$, which couples to the muon, thereby addressing the muon anomalous magnetic moment discrepancy. The model further includes a new heavy lepton, $N$, which serves as a singlet under the Standard Model gauge group but forms a doublet with the muon; this lepton serves as a candidate for dark matter. Theoretical calculations indicate that the model remains consistent with current experimental data and LHC constraints, while also predicting a distinct muon signal.

Coastal and ocean models are essential for investigating climate change impacts and designing effective adaptation strategies. However, their computational intensity often restricts the frequency of data assimilation and the use of uncertainty quantification techniques. To address this limitation, we propose machine learning-based surrogates that can significantly reduce computational costs. We developed a method to train these surrogates using data generated by the HEC-12 model, which simulates storm surges and tsunamis. The resulting models accurately replicate the full model's outputs, enabling faster and more efficient data assimilation and uncertainty quantification.

This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end analysis pipeline designed for the Planck mission, developed by the Planck High Performance Centre (PPHCHPC) at the University of Amsterdam. The project leverages the Planck High Performance Environment (PPHE) framework, a specialized toolkit that enables the execution of complex, computationally intensive tasks on Planck data using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The pipeline's development was supported by a dedicated team of experts in both CMB science and HPC. The resulting code is open-source and publicly accessible, ensuring that the methodology can be adopted by other research groups. The paper details the pipeline's architecture, its specific components, and the procedures for its operation. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive performance analysis of the pipeline, covering the computational resources required, the processing duration, and the resulting data quality. The quality assessment includes a comparison against results generated by the standard CMB pipeline employed by the Planck Collaboration. The findings demonstrate that the pipeline produces results of comparable quality to those of the official CMB pipeline.

This study examines the stability of Turing patterns within a reaction-diffusion system featuring a nonlocal reaction term. We demonstrate that introducing nonlocality into the reaction can destabilize otherwise stable homogeneous states, thereby triggering Turing instability. Furthermore, we establish that the resulting stationary patterns are stable, with their characteristics depending on the nonlocal interaction kernel. To substantiate these findings, we present numerical simulations that illustrate the proposed mechanisms.

We explore a deformation of pure Yang-Mills theory coupled to a phantom field—a scalar field characterized by negative kinetic energy—and identify the phenomenon of super-renormalizability. This occurs because the phantom's negative beta function drives the Yang-Mills coupling toward zero at high energy scales. We further demonstrate that the phantom field effectively cancels the quantum corrections arising within the Yang-Mills sector.

This study examines the polarization characteristics of the photoluminescence (PL) in GaAs/AlGaAs nanowires, with a specific focus on the role of crystal orientation. Our findings indicate that the orientation of the crystal lattice is a decisive factor governing the polarization behavior of PL in these structures. We demonstrate that GaAs/AlGaAs nanowires grown on a (111)B GaAs substrate exhibit a distinct, highly anisotropic PL polarization, a trait that is highly advantageous for developing future photonic devices.

This paper introduces a straightforward Bayesian model designed to infer an opponent's priorities within a multi-issue negotiation setting. The approach utilizes a probabilistic framework to estimate the likelihood of an opponent accepting a specific offer, based on the assumption that acceptance is most probable when the proposed deal aligns with their underlying preference order. To implement this, the method employs a Bayesian network that captures the hierarchical structure of issues and calculates the marginal probability of an opponent's acceptance for each problem variable. We further demonstrate how these networks can be efficiently updated using Clark's algorithm upon receiving a new opponent action. Experimental results indicate that the network-based approach achieves superior performance compared to models lacking a problem-based structure.

This study examines the dynamics of a scalar field within a three-dimensional braneworld scenario, specifically focusing on the existence of stable, localized solutions. Our findings indicate that the scalar field potential is shaped by the dynamical string tension, a parameter arising from the braneworld's dynamics. This newly established tension, which can be either attractive or repulsive, dictates whether strings and matter are confined. We demonstrate that stable domain wall solutions emerge specifically when string confinement is present. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the confinement of strings and the mass of the domain wall, thereby offering a fresh perspective on the interplay between confinement and cosmic structure formation.

This paper introduces a new online field experiment framework designed to sequentially balance covariate information. By integrating the Gittens-Lord-Ziebart (GLZ) approach with online experimentation, our proposed method, OGLZ, dynamically assigns treatments to achieve covariate balance. The GLZ method, originally developed for recommendation systems, ensures that the distribution of covariates across different treatment groups remains consistent. In the context of online field experiments, this balancing is crucial for eliminating selection bias and ensuring that treatment effects are estimated accurately. The GLZ method achieves this by assigning treatments proportionally to the inverse of the discrepancy between an individual unit's covariate profile and the average profile of units already assigned to that treatment group. We apply this method to online field experiments, where we assign treatments proportionally to how much a unit's covariate profile differs from the average profile of previously treated units.

This study presents a comprehensive investigation of the (001)-Si/(001)-$\gamma$-Al$_2$O$_3$ heterointerface, which is identified as the most stable configuration. Utilizing first-principles calculations, we determined that every interfacial silicon atom adopts a four-fold coordination, while interfacial oxygen atoms maintain three-fold coordination. The interface is stabilized by a combination of covalent bonds and ionic interactions, with covalent bonds playing the dominant role. The formation of covalent bonds between interfacial silicon atoms and the Al or Si atoms situated in the first substrate layer is a key factor in stabilizing the interface. Furthermore, the electronic structure reveals a wide band gap of approximately 2.5 eV, with the valence band maximum and conduction band minimum located at the $\Gamma$ point. The band alignment indicates a type-I heterojunction, characterized by the valence band maximum of $\gamma$-Al$_2$O$_3$ lying higher than that of Si, and the conduction band minimum of $\gamma$-Al$_2$O$_3$ lying lower than that of Si.

This work examines the Einstein-axion-dilaton system in four dimensions, focusing on black hole solutions. We employ the method of undetermined coefficients to estimate functions within the field equations, thereby deriving analytic expressions for the axion-dilaton black hole metric. Furthermore, we introduce a novel analytic form of the horizon function for this black hole system, which aligns with the well-known results from the extremal case.

The shipping container crisis was triggered by a convergence of factors, specifically the surge in global trade, the implementation of the Single European Act, containerized shipping's inherent inflexibility, and the rapid expansion of container leasing firms. The container emergency is examined through these lenses, with a specific focus on the impact of the Single European Act.

Anomaly detection in streaming data is a critical area of research with significant applications in diverse domains, including network security, industrial quality control, and healthcare. However, the inherent nonstationarity and high dimensionality of such data present substantial challenges for developing effective detectors. Consequently, the performance of these detectors is primarily governed by two factors: the choice of the underlying probability distribution and the specific strategy used for updating that distribution as new data arrives. This study introduces a novel detector that integrates a mixture of distributions with an online Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to update model parameters in real-time. The proposed method is evaluated against several state-of-the-art detectors using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that the new detector surpasses existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Glioma segmentation is a critical challenge in medical image analysis, directly impacting patient prognosis. While current methods often rely on end-to-end deep learning, they frequently fail to capture the hierarchical nature of gliomas. To address this, we introduce a novel hierarchical network designed to segment the whole tumor and its associated substructures, including the enhancing tumor, tumor core, and edema. Our approach utilizes a multi-task learning strategy that integrates these four segmentation tasks, allowing the model to learn shared features across them. Additionally, we employ a hierarchical loss function to guide the network in learning from coarser to finer structural levels. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the BraTS 2018 dataset, with a specific focus on accurately identifying the enhancing tumor.

This study introduces a novel quantum quasiparticle termed the "triplon," which emerges in frustrated quantum systems exhibiting odd-parity topological order. The concept is illustrated using a spin-1/2 Kagome lattice with a specific exchange interaction, demonstrating that a triplon state can be generated by applying a staggered magnetic field. The research highlights that this quantum entity possesses distinctive properties, including a Berry phase of $2\pi$ and a nontrivial dipole moment. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of phonon coupling on triplons, revealing that they acquire a finite mass when interacting with phonons. These findings offer new avenues for exploring topological quantum states and suggest potential applications in quantum information processing.

This article introduces the concept of statistical convergence utilizing asymptotic density based on $a(n)$, extending previous work on this topic. Furthermore, we examine various properties inherent to this novel form of convergence.

This study examines the convergence properties of a novel second-order, energy-stable, and unconditionally stable numerical approach for solving the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The methodology employs the Crank-Nicolson scheme for temporal discretization, utilizing a specialized technique to linearize the nonlinear terms, while adopting the convolution quadrature approach to address the fourth-order spatial derivative. The primary objective is to derive optimal error bounds under the assumption that the exact solution maintains a constant mean value. The analysis demonstrates that the proposed scheme achieves a third-order convergence rate in time and a fourth-order convergence rate in space. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings.

This study addresses a nonlocal, non-linear fractional elliptic system characterized by the fractional Laplacian, formulated as:
$$
\begin{cases}
(-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u = \lambda u + \mu |\Delta^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u|^{p}|\Delta^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u|^{q} + |u|^{r} & \text{in } \Omega, \\
u = 0 & \text{in } \Omega^c,
\end{cases}
$$
where $\Omega$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Omega^c$ denotes its complement. The parameters satisfy $\alpha \in (0,2)$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$, and the exponents $p, q, r$ are chosen such that $p > 2 - \frac{2}{n}$, $q > 0$, and $rp + qn > 2 - \frac{2}{n}$. The analysis demonstrates the existence of nontrivial weak solutions to this problem for $\lambda > 0$ via the Babuška-Brezzi Theorem. Furthermore, we establish the existence of solutions for $\lambda < 0$ by applying a concentration-compactness argument.

We have identified magnetic exciton Wigner crystallization in charged interlayer excitons within a MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructure subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field. The resulting Wigner crystal manifests as a series of equally spaced, sharp resonances in the photoluminescence spectrum, a pattern that persists even at elevated temperatures. We attribute the thermal resilience of this Wigner crystal to the combined effects of the excitons' reduced effective mass and their enhanced interlayer localization.
